one_liner: Thread-caching malloc replacement for glibc's ptmalloc2; per-thread free lists cut lock contention and per-call cost.
what_it_does: Drop-in replacement for malloc/free/new/delete, linked as -ltcmalloc (or -ltcmalloc_minimal without the heap profiler) or LD_PRELOAD'd over an existing binary, no source changes required. It also bundles an optional heap profiler, heap leak checker, and CPU profiler (output analyzed with the external pprof tool) as separate libraries you can link independently.
how_it_is_fast: Gives each thread a lock-free thread-local cache of free lists spanning ~88 size-classes for objects <=256KB; medium/large objects go through a central page heap and a best-fit red-black tree instead. The allocation/deallocation fast path only touches the thread-local free list, so it takes no locks at all in the common case. A slow-start algorithm resizes each per-thread free list to balance central-list traffic against idle memory, and a build-time --with-tcmalloc-pagesize option trades memory for fewer page-heap operations.
when_to_use: Multi-threaded C++ services with frequent small (<=256KB) alloc/free churn where ptmalloc2 lock contention or per-thread-arena memory stranding is a measured problem
You want the bundled pprof-compatible heap/CPU profiler alongside the allocator, not just a faster malloc
Linux/x86, aarch64, or riscv targets with native TLS, where gperftools documents its fast path as fully optimized
Retrofitting an existing binary via LD_PRELOAD without rebuilding
Workloads that hand large blocks of memory off between phases or threads, where ptmalloc2's per-thread arenas can't reclaim it
when_not_to_use: You need a modern, reproducible speed number vs glibc: the ~6x claim is a 2005-era 32-bit P4 measurement, and the maintainer's Dec 2024 note says glibc has since closed much of that gap
Your code loads the allocator via dlopen(): TCMalloc's initial-exec TLS model breaks under dlopen (documented in INSTALL)
Heavy fork() + multithreading without an immediate exec(): internal locks aren't fully wrapped in pthread_atfork (open issue #1425), so children can hang or profiling data can corrupt on exit()
musl libc targets where you need profiling: backtracing/profiling has repeated musl-specific breakage (issues #1282, #1602, #693); plain malloc is more reliable there
Windows or heap-profiling on non-Linux platforms: Windows support is tcmalloc_minimal only (no heap/CPU profiler), and CMake build support is explicitly called 'preliminary'

integration.dependencies: none for tcmalloc_minimal; full tcmalloc/profiler builds use libunwind (default on most platforms) or built-in backtrace (s390, macOS) for stack unwinding
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (AX_CXX_COMPILE_STDCXX 17 mandatory in configure.ac); autotools (primary, fully supported) or CMake 3.12+ (preliminary); MSVC 2019+ or MinGW for Windows
integration.platforms: x86, aarch64, riscv Linux (primary, fully tested); FreeBSD, NetBSD, macOS (aarch64), Solaris x86, QNX, AIX (partial, per INSTALL); Windows via MSVC 2019+/MinGW limited to tcmalloc_minimal
integration.thread_safety: Thread-safe by design (per-thread caches), but not documented as safe to load via dlopen(), and internal locks are not fully wrapped with pthread_atfork as of the open 2024 issue, so fork()-after-threads has known hang risk
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — true for ordinary link-time or LD_PRELOAD use as a malloc/new replacement, but breaks if loaded via dlopen() and has documented fork-safety caveats

gotchas: Loading via dlopen() breaks tcmalloc's TLS assumptions; it must be linked at startup or LD_PRELOADed, not dlopen'd (INSTALL)
CPU profiling doesn't work correctly across fork() unless the child immediately exec()s; if the child calls exit() instead of _exit(), profile data can be corrupted (README)
--with-tcmalloc-pagesize and CXXFLAGS=-DTCMALLOC_SMALL_BUT_SLOW are build-time, not runtime, speed/memory tradeoffs (INSTALL)
musl libc builds have a history of breakage in backtracing/profiling code across multiple issues; core malloc is more reliable there than the profilers
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick gperftools when you also want its bundled pprof-compatible CPU/heap profiler and are specifically displacing glibc's ptmalloc2 on Linux with a mature, widely-packaged allocator. For a pure allocator-speed decision today, snmalloc and mimalloc publish newer benchmarks claiming wins over tcmalloc itself, so prefer those siblings' Tier B/A evidence over tcmalloc's 2005-era numbers when raw throughput is the deciding factor.
verified_claims_summary: The first-party ~2005 design doc claims ptmalloc2 (glibc 2.3) took ~300ns per small malloc/free pair versus ~50ns for TCMalloc, both measured on a single 2.8 GHz 32-bit Pentium 4, with no compiler, flags, or benchmark harness given. A Dec 2024 maintainer's note in the same document calls those exact numbers obsolete while still asserting gperftools remains somewhat faster than modern glibc.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-05, 8,976 stars, not archived), BSD-3-Clause and small enough to vendor or package; historically used in Chrome/Chromium and widely distributed as libtcmalloc across Linux distros.
